world.bio: I'm Rania, a Lebanese-British woman living in Dubai for over twenty years. I flew as cabin crew for an airline here for six years, then spent fourteen years at the Emirates training college teaching new crew everything from service sequences to emergency procedures to how to smile when your feet hurt. I'm a mother of one teenage son, a dawn runner, and someone who has been on a first-name basis with the Dubai desert for far too long to want to leave. I love the structure of training and the moment a nervous trainee becomes a confident crew member.
skills_assets: Fourteen years as a cabin crew trainer at the Emirates training college, covering service, grooming, safety drills and interview assessment
Six years flying as cabin crew before that, so she knows both sides of the aisle
A thick binder of her own interview assessment sheets, rubrics, role-play scenarios and rewritten scoring guides
Contacts across the Dubai aviation world: former trainees now senior crew, instructors, recruiters
A Dubai residence visa tied to her old employer, expiring in the autumn
A 2019 Nissan she is deciding whether to sell
A running group at 5:15 a.m. in the desert near Al Qudra, six regulars

projects.name: Rewriting assessment sheets
projects.text: Since the July restructuring I have every weekday free and I have caught myself rewriting my old interview assessment sheets at the kitchen table, out of pure habit. The old sheet scored candidates on a one-to-five scale for grooming, communication, teamwork and so on, and I always felt it rewarded confident talkers rather than people who would be calm at 3 a.m. over the Atlantic. The new version has scenario questions and a column for observed behaviour under mild stress. It has no home and no purpose. I just keep improving it. I printed six copies and ran them past two old colleagues, who said they were better than the college's own.

projects.name: Son's university applications
projects.text: Karim is seventeen and applying to universities in the UK: Manchester, Leeds, Edinburgh, and a long shot at UCL. Personal statement is due 15 October. Costs weigh heavily now that my salary has gone. I'm trying not to show him the worry.

notes.text: Sat at the kitchen table again at 9 a.m. with coffee, and no one to train. Used to be that by this hour I'd have run two sessions and a debrief. Pulled out the interview sheet instead. Changed 'Appearance: 1-5' to something more honest. Still thinking about what 'honest' means for an airline that wants a particular look.

Desert run at 5:15 with the group. Salma and Ben were late, as always. The sun came up pink over the dunes and for twenty minutes I forgot I had no job. Then Ben asked 'so what are you doing now?' and I said 'resting.' Which is a lie I tell very well.

Karim's personal statement draft. He writes about wanting to be an engineer but the real story is about moving countries and being the only kid with an accent in every classroom. I told him to write that. He rolled his eyes. He will, in the end.

Looked at the car insurance renewal. 3,400 dirhams. If I sell the Nissan I could cover two months of rent. If I sell it, I can't take Karim to the airport. Silly thing to cry about. Cried a bit anyway.

Two former trainees messaged me today. One is now a purser, the other is in Frankfurt, flying long haul. Both said the same thing: 'we still use what you taught us.' It is good to hear. It does not pay rent.
Visa runs out on 30 November unless I find new sponsorship or a different arrangement. I have been telling myself it's fine. It isn't fine. I am not telling anyone, including my sister in London.

Looked at the assessment sheet again. One column I'm proud of: 'What does the candidate do when they don't know the answer?' Most sheets ignore this. In 14 years it was the best predictor of who'd be good in a real emergency. I wish someone would ask me to explain why.

Went to the mall to buy Karim a winter coat for the UK. Felt ridiculous standing in a shop with 38-degree weather outside. Bought the coat anyway, on credit card. Then sat in the car park for ten minutes.
Decided: I'm staying in Dubai. Not leaving until Karim's results come out in the spring, whatever happens. It sounds brave. It's just stubbornness.

messages.text:
Karim: Mum, can you read my statement tonight?
Me: Of course. Send it after dinner.
Karim: It's bad.
Me: Everyone's first draft is bad. That's what drafts are for.

Salma: Are you coming Saturday? We're doing the long loop.
Me: Yes, I'll bring dates.
Salma: And a coffee flask? Pleeease.
Me: Deal.

Hannah: Heard about the restructuring. I'm so sorry, Rania. You were the best trainer we had.
Me: Thank you. I'm all right. Just figuring things out.
Hannah: If you want a reference, anything, I'm here.
Me: Appreciate that.

Sister: Come to London for a few weeks? Karim could see the universities.
Me: I can't leave right now. Maybe at Christmas.
Sister: Rania, you sound tired.
Me: I'm fine. Really.

Faisal: I can offer 28,000 for the Nissan.
Me: I'll think about it.
Faisal: Offer stands until Friday.
